notes.objective: Explain what IaC is
notes.title: Infrastructure as code in one idea
notes.gist: You describe servers, networks and services in text files, and a tool builds and updates the real thing to match.
points: IaC replaces console clicks with configuration files you version, reuse and share.
Terraform is declarative: you state the end result, not step-by-step commands.
Files live in Git, so every change has history, review and rollback.
Terraform manages low-level parts like compute and storage and high-level ones like DNS.
The same code applied again gives the same result: consistent, repeatable environments.

notes.objective: Describe the advantages of IaC patterns
notes.title: Why IaC beats manual changes
notes.gist: Code makes infrastructure repeatable, reviewable and automatable, so teams move faster with fewer mistakes and less drift.
points: Version control: see who changed what and roll back a bad change.
Reuse: modules package proven patterns so teams stop rebuilding the same thing.
Plan before apply: preview every create, update and destroy first.
Automation: run the same workflow in CI/CD for every environment.
Terraform builds a dependency graph and creates independent resources in parallel.
notes.tip: Benefit questions want versioning, reuse, consistency and automation. Reject options claiming IaC removes the need for state or guarantees lower cloud bills.

flowchart TB

  C --> F

notes.objective: Explain how Terraform manages multi-cloud, hybrid cloud, and service-agnostic workflows
notes.title: One workflow for any cloud
notes.gist: Providers translate the same language and the same init, plan, apply loop into calls to any platform with an API.
points: Each platform has a provider plugin; the Registry lists thousands of them.
One configuration can mix AWS, Azure, GCP, on-prem and SaaS providers.
Cross-cloud dependencies work: one provider's output feeds another provider's resource.
Multi-cloud improves fault tolerance, but each cloud keeps its own resource types.
Service-agnostic means DNS, monitoring, Git or Kubernetes too, not only VMs.
notes.tip: Terraform does not make code portable between clouds. The workflow and language are shared, but resources such as `aws_instance` are provider-specific.

summary.tests: Whether you can explain what infrastructure as code is, why it beats manual changes, and how one Terraform workflow covers many clouds and services.
must_know: IaC means defining infrastructure in files you version, reuse and share.
Terraform is declarative: you describe the end state, it works out the steps.
Benefits: version history, code review, reuse via modules, plan previews, automation in CI/CD.
State acts as the source of truth for what Terraform manages.
Providers let the same language and workflow drive any platform with an API.
One configuration can mix cloud, on-prem and SaaS providers with cross-provider references.
traps: Thinking Terraform makes code portable: an `aws_instance` never deploys to Azure.
Calling Terraform procedural; scripts and runbooks are procedural, Terraform is declarative.
Treating manual console changes as fine alongside IaC; they cause drift.

cards.q: What does infrastructure as code (IaC) mean?
cards.a: Defining infrastructure in configuration files that you version, reuse and share, instead of clicking in a console.

cards.q: In Terraform's declarative model, what do you write and what does Terraform work out?
cards.a: You describe the end state; Terraform works out the steps to reach it.

cards.q: Which five benefits of IaC does the exam expect you to name?
cards.a: Version history, code review, reuse via modules, plan previews, and automation in CI/CD.

cards.q: What acts as the source of truth for what Terraform manages?
cards.a: State: Terraform's record of which real object each resource block owns.

cards.q: What lets the same Terraform language and workflow drive any platform that has an API?
cards.a: Providers. They translate the same language and init, plan, apply loop into calls to that platform's API.

cards.q: Can one configuration mix cloud, on-prem and SaaS providers, and can they reference each other?
cards.a: Yes. One configuration can mix them, and one provider's output can feed another provider's resource.

cards.q: Trap: does Terraform make code portable, so an `aws_instance` can deploy to Azure?
cards.a: No. The workflow and language are shared, but resources like `aws_instance` are provider-specific and never deploy to Azure.

cards.q: Trap: a question calls Terraform procedural. Which approaches are actually procedural?
cards.a: Shell scripts and runbooks are procedural. Terraform is declarative: you state the end result, not step-by-step commands.

cards.q: Trap: are manual console changes fine alongside IaC?
cards.a: No. They cause drift, and they are the anti-pattern IaC removes.

cards.q: How does Terraform create resources that do not depend on each other?
cards.a: It builds a dependency graph and creates independent resources in parallel.

cards.q: Trap: an answer option says IaC removes the need for state or guarantees lower cloud bills. Is it right?
cards.a: No. Reject both claims; benefit questions want versioning, reuse, consistency and automation.

cards.q: What does service-agnostic mean for Terraform's reach beyond virtual machines?
cards.a: It also manages things like DNS, monitoring, Git or Kubernetes, not only VMs.

cards.q: What does a multi-cloud Terraform setup improve?
cards.a: Fault tolerance. Each cloud still keeps its own resource types.

notes.objective: Install and version Terraform providers
notes.title: Install and pin provider versions
notes.gist: Declare each provider in `required_providers`, let `terraform init` download it, and the lock file freezes the exact version.
points: Give each provider a `source` such as `hashicorp/aws` and a `version` constraint.
Source address is `[hostname/]namespace/type`; hostname defaults to `registry.terraform.io`.
`~> 1.2.0` allows only 1.2.x patches; root modules should cap the maximum version.
`.terraform.lock.hcl` records chosen versions and checksums; commit it to Git.
`terraform init -upgrade` ignores the lock and picks the newest allowed version.
notes.tip: The lock file covers providers only, not modules. A plain `init` keeps the locked version even when a newer one exists; only `-upgrade` moves it.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[required providers + version] --> B[terraform init]
  B --> C[Registry download]
  C --> D[.terraform/providers]
  B --> E[.terraform.lock.hcl]
  E -->|commit to Git| F[Same version for team]
  G[init -upgrade] -.->|newest allowed| E

video.title: Terraform Lock File

notes.objective: Describe how Terraform uses providers
notes.title: Providers: plugins that talk to APIs
notes.gist: Terraform core reads your config, builds the graph and tracks state; provider plugins make the actual API calls for each platform.
points: Core and providers are separate binaries that talk over RPC.
Providers authenticate, define resources and data sources, and can add functions.
A `provider` block sets options like region; omit it and an empty default is used.
Registry tiers: Official, Partner Premier, Partner, Community; Archived means no longer maintained.
Add or change a provider and you must run `terraform init` again.
notes.tip: Providers are plugins, not part of the `terraform` binary, so `init` must install them first. If none is installed locally, init fetches the newest version allowed.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[.tf config] --> B[Terraform core]
  B -->|RPC| C[Provider plugin]
  C -->|auth + API calls| D[(Cloud API)]
  B --> E[Resource graph]
  B --> F[(State)]

notes.objective: Write Terraform configuration using multiple providers
notes.title: Multiple providers and aliases
notes.gist: List every provider you need, and use `alias` when you need two setups of the same provider, such as two regions.
points: Add a second `provider` block for the same provider with a unique `alias`, e.g. `west`.
Pick it per resource or data source with `provider = aws.west`.
The block without `alias` is the default configuration for that provider.
Pass aliases into child modules with the `providers = { aws = aws.west }` map.
Different providers, like `aws` and `random`, sit together in one configuration without aliases.
notes.tip: The reference is `aws.west`, not `aws.alias.west` or a quoted string. Resources without a `provider` argument always use the default, unaliased configuration.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[provider aws default] --> R1[resource in us-east-1]
  B[provider aws alias west] --> R2[resource with provider = aws.west]
  B --> M[module with providers map]
  C[provider random] --> R3[random password]

notes.objective: Explain how Terraform uses and manages state
notes.title: State maps code to real resources
notes.gist: State is Terraform's record of which real object each resource block owns, plus metadata it needs to plan the next change.
points: Default is a JSON `terraform.tfstate` file written by the local backend.
Maps `aws_instance.web` to a real ID like `i-abcd1234`: one object, one address.
Stores dependencies so resources deleted from config are destroyed in the right order.
Caches attribute values; by default plan refreshes them from the real world.
Teams use remote state so everyone works from one shared, locked copy.
notes.tip: State is required, not optional, and can hold secrets in plain text. Never hand-edit it; use `terraform state` commands or `moved`, `removed` and `import` blocks.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Config: desired] --> P{terraform plan}
  S[(State: last known)] --> P
  R[(Real infrastructure)] -->|refresh| P
  P --> X[apply]
  X --> S

video.title: Managing Terraform State Files

summary.tests: How providers are declared, installed, pinned and configured, including aliases, and why Terraform needs a state file.
must_know: Declare providers in `required_providers` with a `source` and a `version` constraint.
`~>` lets only the rightmost version part rise; `>=` sets a minimum.
`terraform init` downloads providers; `.terraform.lock.hcl` pins versions and checksums. Commit it.
Run `terraform init -upgrade` to move past a locked version.
Use `alias` for a second configuration of one provider; select it with `provider = aws.west`.
State maps each resource address to one real object and stores dependency metadata.
traps: Believing the lock file pins module versions; it tracks providers only.
Writing `aws.alias.west` or a quoted string instead of `aws.west`.
Assuming state is optional or that it hides secrets; it is required and stores them in plain text.

cards.q: Where do you declare the providers a configuration needs, and which two arguments does each one take?
cards.a: In `required_providers`, giving each provider a `source` such as `hashicorp/aws` and a `version` constraint.

cards.q: In a version constraint, which operator lets only the rightmost version part rise, and which sets a minimum?
cards.a: `~>` lets only the rightmost part rise (`~> 1.2.0` allows only 1.2.x patches); `>=` sets a minimum.

cards.q: Which file records the chosen provider versions and checksums, and should it go in Git?
cards.a: `.terraform.lock.hcl`. Commit it to Git so the whole team gets the same provider version.

cards.q: Which command downloads the providers a configuration needs?
cards.a: `terraform init`. Add or change a provider and you must run it again.

cards.q: How do you move a provider past the version pinned in the lock file?
cards.a: Run `terraform init -upgrade`: it ignores the lock and picks the newest allowed version. A plain `init` keeps the locked version.

cards.q: How do you set up a second configuration of one provider, such as another region, and select it on a resource?
cards.a: Add another `provider` block with a unique `alias`, such as `west`, then set `provider = aws.west` on the resource.

cards.q: What does Terraform state map, and what extra metadata does it store?
cards.a: It maps each resource address, such as `aws_instance.web`, to one real object, and stores dependency metadata.

cards.q: Trap: does the lock file pin module versions?
cards.a: No. `.terraform.lock.hcl` tracks providers only, not modules.

cards.q: Trap: how do you reference the provider alias `west` of `aws` on a resource?
cards.a: `provider = aws.west`. Not `aws.alias.west`, and not a quoted string.

cards.q: Trap: is state optional, and does it hide secrets?
cards.a: No to both. State is required and stores secrets in plain text. Never hand-edit it.

cards.q: What is the format of a provider source address, and what is the default hostname?
cards.a: `[hostname/]namespace/type`; the hostname defaults to `registry.terraform.io`.

cards.q: Which provider configuration does a resource with no `provider` argument use?
cards.a: The default, unaliased configuration.

cards.q: How do you pass an aliased provider into a child module?
cards.a: With the `providers` map in the module block: `providers = { aws = aws.west }`.

cards.q: What is the default state file, and which backend writes it?
cards.a: A JSON file named `terraform.tfstate`, written by the local backend.

notes.objective: Describe the Terraform workflow
notes.title: Write, plan, apply loop
notes.gist: You write config, preview the change with a plan, then apply it, and repeat that loop for every change.
points: Core loop: Write, Plan, Apply; `terraform init` comes first to install providers and modules.
Teams write on Git branches and review speculative plan output in pull requests.
Re-check the final plan after merge; reality may have changed since review.
HCP Terraform runs the same loop remotely with shared state and variables.
`terraform apply` shows a plan and waits for `yes` unless `-auto-approve`.
notes.tip: Ordering questions: `init`, then `plan`, then `apply`. `validate` and `fmt` are helpful extras, not one of the three core workflow stages.

  I --> P[terraform plan]
  P --> R{Reviewed OK?}

source.title: Overview of the core Terraform workflow

notes.objective: Initialize a Terraform working directory
notes.title: terraform init prepares the folder
notes.gist: `init` sets up the backend, downloads providers and modules, and writes the lock file; running it again is always safe.
points: First command after writing or cloning config; it never deletes config or state.
Creates `.terraform/` with providers, modules and backend settings; keep it out of Git.
`-upgrade` moves providers and modules to the newest allowed versions.
`-migrate-state` copies state to a new backend; `-reconfigure` ignores the old one.
`-backend=false` skips backend setup; `-backend-config` fills in partial backend settings.
notes.tip: Rerun `init` after adding a provider, changing a module source or version, or changing the backend. Errors saying a module or provider is not installed point here.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  I[terraform init] --> B[Configure backend]
  I --> P[Download providers]
  I --> M[Download modules]
  P --> L[.terraform.lock.hcl]
  B --> D[.terraform folder]
  M --> D

notes.objective: Validate a Terraform configuration
notes.title: terraform validate checks the code
notes.gist: `validate` confirms the configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent, without calling any cloud API or reading state.
points: Catches typos, wrong attribute names, wrong value types and missing required arguments.
Does not check remote services, credentials or whether resources would really succeed.
Needs an initialized directory; `terraform init -backend=false` is enough.
Works regardless of variable values or existing state, so it suits reusable modules.
`-json` gives machine-readable results for editors and CI.
notes.tip: Any option saying `validate` detects drift, expired credentials or API quota problems is wrong. It only inspects the code itself.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[.tf files] --> V[terraform validate]
  V --> B{Syntax and types OK?}
  B -->|yes| C[Success, no API calls]
  B -->|no| D[Error with file and line]

notes.objective: Generate and review an execution plan for Terraform
notes.title: Read the plan before applying
notes.gist: `plan` refreshes state, compares it with your config, and lists what it would create, change or destroy, without changing anything.
points: Symbols: `+` create, `~` update in place, `-` destroy, `<=` read a data source.
`-out=tfplan` saves the plan; `terraform apply tfplan` runs exactly that plan.
Without `-out` you get a speculative plan, for review only.
`-refresh-only` shows drift, `-replace=ADDR` forces replacement, `-target` narrows scope.
`-/+` destroys then recreates; `+/-` creates the replacement first (`create_before_destroy`).
notes.tip: A plan never changes infrastructure. `-target` is for exceptional recovery, not routine use. `plan -destroy` previews exactly what `terraform destroy` would do.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C[Config] --> P[terraform plan]
  S[(State)] --> P
  R[(Real resources)] -->|refresh| P
  P --> O[Diff: add, change, destroy]
  P -->|saved with out flag| F[Saved plan file]
  F --> A[terraform apply tfplan]

notes.objective: Apply changes to infrastructure with Terraform
notes.title: terraform apply makes it real
notes.gist: `apply` carries out a plan, either a fresh one it shows you for approval or a saved plan file, then updates state.
points: Without a plan file it builds a plan, asks for `yes`, then acts.
`-auto-approve` skips the prompt; use only in trusted automation.
A saved plan file runs with no prompt and accepts no extra planning options.
Inspect a saved plan with `terraform show tfplan` before applying.
Without a plan file it accepts `-replace`, `-target`, `-var` and `-refresh-only` like plan.
notes.tip: Passing a saved plan counts as approval, so `-auto-approve` is ignored. You cannot add `-var` or `-target` when applying a saved plan file.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A{Plan file given?} -->|no| B[Make new plan]
  B --> C[Prompt for yes]
  A -->|yes| D[Run saved plan, no prompt]
  C --> E[Call provider APIs]
  D --> E
  E --> F[(State updated)]

notes.objective: Destroy Terraform-managed infrastructure
notes.title: terraform destroy removes managed resources
notes.gist: `destroy` plans and deletes every resource tracked in the current state, and leaves anything Terraform does not manage alone.
points: `terraform destroy` is a shortcut for `terraform apply -destroy`.
Preview it first with `terraform plan -destroy`.
It asks for `yes`; `-auto-approve` skips the prompt.
`-target=ADDR` limits the destroy to one resource and its dependencies.
`lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` makes any plan destroying that resource fail.
notes.tip: Destroy only touches objects in state. Deleting a block from config and applying also destroys it; use a `removed` block with `destroy = false` to just forget it.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[terraform destroy] --> B[Plan: destroy all in state]
  B --> C{Approve yes?}
  C -->|yes| D[Delete in dependency order]
  D --> E[(Empty state)]
  F[prevent destroy set] -.->|blocks| B

notes.objective: Apply formatting and style adjustments to a configuration
notes.title: terraform fmt for canonical style
notes.gist: `fmt` rewrites .tf files into HashiCorp's canonical style; it is deliberately opinionated and has no style options.
points: Formats the current directory only; add `-recursive` for subfolders.
`-check` changes nothing and exits non-zero if files need formatting: ideal for CI.
`-diff` shows the changes; `-write=false` stops it overwriting files.
Changes layout only, never meaning; it does not validate logic.
Rerun it after upgrading Terraform, as the canonical format can shift slightly.
notes.tip: Classic trap: `fmt` does not recurse by default. For a pipeline gate that fails on bad style, the answer is `terraform fmt -check`, often with `-recursive`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[.tf files] --> F[terraform fmt]
  F --> B[Files rewritten in place]
  A --> C[terraform fmt -check]
  C --> D{Formatted?}
  D -->|no| E[Non-zero exit, CI fails]
  D -->|yes| G[Exit 0]

summary.tests: The order and purpose of init, validate, plan, apply, destroy and fmt, and the key flags each command takes.
must_know: Core loop is Write, Plan, Apply; `terraform init` must run first.
`init` sets up backend, providers, modules and lock file; it is safe to rerun.
`validate` checks syntax and internal consistency only, with no API or state access.
`plan -out=tfplan` saves a plan; `apply tfplan` runs it with no prompt.
`terraform destroy` equals `terraform apply -destroy`; preview with `plan -destroy`.
`fmt -check` fails CI on bad style; add `-recursive` for subfolders.
Plan modes and options: `-refresh-only`, `-replace`, `-target`, `-var`, `-var-file`.
traps: Thinking `validate` catches bad credentials, drift or API errors.
Forgetting `fmt` only formats the current directory unless you add `-recursive`.
Expecting `-auto-approve` to matter with a saved plan; the plan file is already the approval.

cards.q: What are the three core workflow stages, and which command must run first?
cards.a: Write, Plan, Apply. Run `terraform init` first to install providers and modules.

cards.q: What does `terraform init` set up, and is it safe to run again?
cards.a: It sets up the backend, providers, modules and lock file. Rerunning is always safe; it never deletes config or state.

cards.q: What does `terraform validate` check, and what does it not touch?
cards.a: Syntax and internal consistency only. It makes no API calls and does not read state.

cards.q: How do you save a plan and then run exactly that plan?
cards.a: `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, then `terraform apply tfplan`. A saved plan runs with no prompt.

cards.q: Which `apply` flag is `terraform destroy` a shortcut for, and how do you preview a destroy?
cards.a: `terraform apply -destroy`. Preview it with `terraform plan -destroy`.

cards.q: Which `fmt` flag fails a CI pipeline on bad style without rewriting files?
cards.a: `terraform fmt -check`: it changes nothing and exits non-zero when files need formatting.

cards.q: Which plan option shows drift, which forces replacement of one resource, and which narrows scope?
cards.a: `-refresh-only` shows drift, `-replace=ADDR` forces replacement, and `-target` narrows the scope.

cards.q: Trap: does `terraform validate` catch bad credentials, drift or API errors?
cards.a: No. It inspects only the code itself: no remote services, no credentials, no drift.

cards.q: Trap: which directories does `terraform fmt` format by default?
cards.a: Only the current directory. Add `-recursive` to format subfolders.

cards.q: Trap: what does `-auto-approve` do when you apply a saved plan file?
cards.a: Nothing; it is ignored. Passing a saved plan already counts as approval.

cards.q: In plan output, what do the symbols `+`, `~`, `-` and `<=` mean?
cards.a: `+` create, `~` update in place, `-` destroy, `<=` read a data source.

cards.q: In plan output, which symbol means destroy then recreate, and which creates the replacement first?
cards.a: `-/+` destroys then recreates; `+/-` creates the replacement first (`create_before_destroy`).

cards.q: Which resources does `terraform destroy` delete?
cards.a: Every resource tracked in the current state. Anything Terraform does not manage is left alone.

cards.q: Without a plan file, which planning options does `apply` accept?
cards.a: `-replace`, `-target`, `-var` and `-refresh-only`, like `plan`. A saved plan file accepts no extra planning options.

notes.objective: Use and differentiate `resource` and `data` blocks
notes.title: Resources create, data sources read
notes.gist: A `resource` block makes Terraform create and manage an object; a `data` block only reads something that already exists.
points: `resource` blocks take a type and a local name, e.g. `aws_instance` and `web`.
Reference data as `data.<TYPE>.<NAME>.<ATTR>`, e.g. `data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id`.
Data sources are read-only; Terraform never creates, updates or deletes them.
Reads happen at plan time unless arguments depend on values known only after apply.
Both accept meta-arguments such as `count`, `for_each`, `provider` and `depends_on`.

notes.objective: Refer to resource attributes and create cross-resource references
notes.title: Referencing attributes across resources
notes.gist: Write `TYPE.NAME.ATTRIBUTE` to use one resource's value in another, and Terraform learns which to build first.
points: Resource `aws_instance.web.id`, variable `var.x`, local `local.x`, module output `module.net.vpc_id`.
With `count` the reference is a list: `aws_instance.web[0].id`.
With `for_each` it is a map: `aws_instance.web["a"].id`.
Splat `aws_instance.web[*].id` returns every instance's ID as a list.
Special values: `count.index`, `each.key`, `each.value`, `self`, `path.module`, `terraform.workspace`.
notes.tip: A reference creates an implicit dependency automatically. `for_each` instances are keyed by string, so indexing them with `[0]` is a wrong answer.

  S -->|subnet id| I[aws instance web]

notes.objective: Use variables and outputs
notes.title: Input variables, locals and outputs
notes.gist: Variables are a module's inputs, locals are named helper expressions inside it, and outputs are its return values.
points: `variable` accepts `type`, `default`, `description`, `validation`, `sensitive`, `nullable`, `ephemeral`.
Precedence, highest first: `-var`/`-var-file`, `*.auto.tfvars`, `terraform.tfvars.json`, `terraform.tfvars`, `TF_VAR_` env, `default`.
No default and no value supplied means Terraform prompts for it.
`output` exposes values to the CLI, parent modules and `terraform_remote_state`.
Read outputs with `terraform output`; `-raw` and `-json` print sensitive values in plain text.
notes.tip: Precedence trap: environment variables lose to every tfvars file, and CLI flags win. `terraform.tfvars` loads automatically, but `prod.tfvars` needs `-var-file`.

notes.objective: Understand and use complex types
notes.title: Complex types: lists, maps, sets, objects
notes.gist: Collection types hold many values of one type; structural types let each attribute or position have its own type.
points: `list(string)`: ordered, indexed from zero, every element the same type.
`map(number)`: string keys pointing to values of one type.
`set(string)`: unique values with no order and no index.
`object({ name = string, age = number })`: named attributes, each with its own type.
`tuple([string, number, bool])`: fixed positions, each with its own type.
notes.tip: `map` has one value type while `object` has a schema. A set has no index, so `[0]` on it fails. Avoid `any` unless you only pass values through.

  S --> O[object: named attributes]

notes.objective: Write dynamic configuration using expressions and functions
notes.title: Expressions, loops and built-in functions
notes.gist: Use conditionals, `for` expressions, `count`, `for_each`, `dynamic` blocks and built-in functions to generate config instead of copying it.
points: Conditional: `var.env == "prod" ? 3 : 1`.
`count = 3` makes instances `[0]` to `[2]`; `for_each` takes a map or set of strings.
`for_each` keys must be known at plan time and cannot be sensitive.
`dynamic` blocks with a `content` body generate repeated nested blocks like `ingress`.
Only built-in or provider functions exist, e.g. `merge`, `join`; try them in `terraform console`.
notes.tip: Removing a middle item from a `count` list shifts indexes and recreates later resources; `for_each` keys avoid that churn. You cannot write user-defined functions.

notes.objective: Define resource dependencies in configuration
notes.title: Implicit and explicit dependencies
notes.gist: Terraform orders work from the references between resources; add `depends_on` only when a dependency is hidden from it.
points: Referencing another resource's attribute creates an implicit dependency automatically.
`depends_on = [aws_s3_bucket.logs]` declares a hidden one, like an app using a bucket.
Independent resources are built in parallel, up to 10 at a time by default.
Dependencies also set destroy order, which runs in reverse.
`terraform graph` prints the dependency graph for visualising.
notes.tip: Prefer references over `depends_on`; `depends_on` makes plans more conservative and hides intent. `depends_on` lists whole resources or modules, not attribute values.

notes.objective: Validate configuration using custom conditions
notes.title: Validation, pre/postconditions and checks
notes.gist: Custom conditions stop bad inputs or broken assumptions early, while `check` blocks only warn about the health of live infrastructure.
points: `validation { condition, error_message }` inside a `variable` checks input values at plan.
`precondition` checks assumptions on resources, data sources and outputs before creation.
`postcondition` checks guarantees after apply or after a data source read.
`check` blocks with `assert` run as the last step and only warn.
Every condition needs an `error_message` explaining the failure.
notes.tip: Need a failure that blocks the run? Validation or a pre/postcondition. Need a warning that never blocks, like an HTTP health check? A `check` block, Terraform 1.5+.

notes.title: Secrets: sensitive, ephemeral and Vault
notes.gist: `sensitive` only hides values from output; to keep secrets safe, use ephemeral values, fetch them from Vault and protect state.
points: `sensitive = true` redacts values in plan and apply output and the HCP UI.
Sensitive values are still stored in plain text in state and plan files.
`ephemeral = true` (1.10+) and write-only arguments (1.11+) keep values out of state.
The Vault provider reads secrets at run time instead of hard-coding them in `.tf`.
Protect state: encrypted remote backend, tight access, never commit `terraform.tfstate`.
notes.tip: Classic trap: marking a variable `sensitive` does not encrypt it or keep it out of state. `terraform output -json` or `-raw` still prints it in clear text.

notes.title: Lifecycle rules and provisioners
notes.gist: The `lifecycle` block changes how Terraform replaces or protects a resource; provisioners run scripts and are a last resort.
points: `create_before_destroy = true` builds the replacement first, then deletes the old one.
`prevent_destroy = true` rejects any plan that would destroy the resource.
`ignore_changes = [tags]` stops Terraform reverting outside edits to those attributes.
`replace_triggered_by` replaces a resource when a referenced item changes.
`local-exec` and `remote-exec` are a last resort; `terraform_data` hosts them without a provider.
notes.tip: `prevent_destroy` only protects while the block stays in config. A failed creation-time provisioner marks the resource tainted, so the next apply recreates it.

flowchart TB

must_know: `resource` creates and manages; `data` only reads, as `data.TYPE.NAME.ATTR`.
References like `aws_vpc.main.id` create implicit dependencies; `depends_on` is for hidden ones.
Variable precedence, highest first: CLI flags, `*.auto.tfvars`, `terraform.tfvars`, `TF_VAR_` env, `default`.
`for_each` takes a map or set of strings known at plan time; `count` takes a number.
Validation and pre/postconditions stop the run; `check` blocks only warn.
`sensitive = true` hides output but values still sit in state; `ephemeral` keeps them out.
Only built-in and provider functions exist; there are no user-defined functions.
traps: Using `count` for a list of distinct items, then deleting one and recreating everything after it.
Believing `sensitive` encrypts a value or removes it from state.
Expecting environment variables to beat `terraform.tfvars`; they rank below every tfvars file.

cards.q: Which block creates and manages an object, and which one only reads an existing one?
cards.a: `resource` creates and manages; `data` only reads, and is referenced as `data.<TYPE>.<NAME>.<ATTR>`.

cards.q: How does Terraform learn the build order, and when do you add `depends_on`?
cards.a: A reference like `aws_vpc.main.id` creates an implicit dependency; add `depends_on` only for a dependency Terraform cannot see.

cards.q: List variable value precedence from highest to lowest.
cards.a: `-var`/`-var-file`, `*.auto.tfvars`, `terraform.tfvars.json`, `terraform.tfvars`, `TF_VAR_` env, then `default`.

cards.q: What does `for_each` take as input, and what does `count` take?
cards.a: `for_each` takes a map or set of strings known at plan time; `count` takes a number.

cards.q: Which custom conditions stop the run, and which one only warns?
cards.a: Variable validation, `precondition` and `postcondition` stop the run. `check` blocks with `assert` only warn (Terraform 1.5+).

cards.q: What does `sensitive = true` do, and what keeps a value out of state?
cards.a: It only redacts output; the value is still in state in plain text. `ephemeral = true` (1.10+) keeps values out of state.

cards.q: Can you write your own functions in Terraform configuration?
cards.a: No. Only built-in and provider functions exist, such as `merge` and `join`; try them in `terraform console`.

cards.q: Trap: what happens when you delete a middle item from a `count` list of distinct items?
cards.a: Indexes shift, so every later resource is recreated. `for_each` keys avoid that churn.

cards.q: Trap: does marking a variable `sensitive` encrypt it or remove it from state?
cards.a: No. It only hides the value in output. It stays in state and plan files, and `terraform output -json` or `-raw` still prints it.

cards.q: Trap: a value is set in both a `TF_VAR_` environment variable and `terraform.tfvars`. Which wins?
cards.a: The tfvars file. Environment variables rank below every tfvars file; CLI flags win over all of them.

cards.a: `terraform.tfvars` loads automatically; `prod.tfvars` needs `-var-file`.

cards.q: By default, how many independent resources does Terraform build in parallel?
cards.a: Up to 10 at a time.

cards.q: Which `lifecycle` setting makes any plan that would destroy a resource fail, and when does it stop protecting?
cards.a: `prevent_destroy = true`. It protects only while the block stays in config.

cards.a: `map` has one value type for all keys; `object` has a schema of named attributes, each with its own type.

notes.objective: Explain how Terraform sources modules
notes.title: Where modules come from
notes.gist: The `source` argument tells `terraform init` where to fetch a module: a local folder, a registry, a Git repository or an archive.
points: Local: `./modules/vpc` or `../shared`; nothing is downloaded and no `version` allowed.
Public registry: `<NAMESPACE>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER>`, e.g. `hashicorp/consul/aws`.
Private registry adds a host: `app.terraform.io/<ORG>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER>`.
Git: `git::https://example.com/vpc.git?ref=v1.2.0`; `//` selects a subfolder.
`source` must be a literal string; rerun `terraform init` after changing it.
notes.tip: Registry addresses have three parts ending in the provider name. `source` cannot use variables. Partner modules on the Registry are reviewed by HashiCorp.

notes.objective: Describe variable scope within modules
notes.title: Module scope: inputs in, outputs out
notes.gist: Each module is a sealed box: it sees only its own variables, locals and resources, and shares data only through outputs.
points: A child cannot read the parent's `var.` or `local.` values directly.
The parent passes values as arguments in the `module` block, matching child `variable` names.
The parent reads child data only through `module.<NAME>.<OUTPUT>`.
Locals are private to the module that defines them.
Children inherit default provider configurations; pass aliases with `providers`.
notes.tip: If a child needs a value, declare a `variable` in the child and pass it in. Referencing `module.net.aws_vpc.main.id` is invalid; expose it as an output.

notes.objective: Use modules in configuration
notes.title: Calling and composing modules
notes.gist: Add a `module` block with a source and inputs, wire outputs between modules in the root, and keep the tree flat.
points: One source in two `module` blocks with different labels gives two independent copies.
`count`, `for_each`, `depends_on` and `providers` work on `module` blocks.
Wire modules in the root: `vpc_id = module.network.vpc_id`.
HashiCorp recommends one level of child modules: composition over deep nesting.
Run `terraform init` after adding a module so it gets installed.
notes.tip: Module composition means the root passes dependencies in, rather than a module creating its own copy. One module cannot see another's resources without outputs.

points: `version = "~> 5.1"` works only for registry sources, public or private.
Git sources pin with `?ref=v1.2.0` in the URL instead.
The lock file does not record module versions; init picks the newest match.
Use an exact version constraint when you need the same module version every time.
`terraform init -upgrade` fetches newer module versions within the constraint.

cards.q: Which module sources accept `version`, and how does a Git source pin a version?

notes.objective: Describe the local backend
notes.title: Local backend and CLI workspaces
notes.gist: By default Terraform keeps state in `terraform.tfstate` on your disk, locks it with system APIs, and runs everything locally.
points: Used when there is no `backend` or `cloud` block; it is the default.
Optional `path` argument moves the file; default is `terraform.tfstate` in the root module.
`terraform workspace new dev` gives a separate state per CLI workspace.
`terraform.workspace` returns the current name; the `default` workspace cannot be deleted.
Fine for one person; teams need a shared remote backend.
notes.tip: CLI workspaces split state under one backend; they are not HCP Terraform workspaces and are not suitable when environments need separate credentials or access control.

notes.objective: Describe state locking
notes.title: State locking stops concurrent writes
notes.gist: When the backend supports it, Terraform locks state during any write so two people cannot change it at the same time.
points: Locking is automatic on every operation that could write state, with no message.
Not all backends lock; local uses system APIs, S3 uses `use_lockfile = true`.
S3 locking through DynamoDB is deprecated in favour of the S3 lock file.
`-lock-timeout=60s` waits for a lock; the default `0s` fails immediately.
`terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID` clears a stuck lock; use only for your own lock.
notes.tip: `-lock=false` and `force-unlock` are dangerous escape hatches, not fixes for normal contention. If Terraform cannot get the lock, it stops rather than continuing.

  B[User B: apply] -->|lock held| W[Wait or error]

notes.objective: Configure remote state using the backend block
notes.title: Remote state with a backend block
notes.gist: A `backend` block inside `terraform {}` stores state remotely, such as in S3, so a team shares one locked copy.
points: One `backend` block per configuration; it cannot use variables, locals or data sources.
Partial config: leave values out and pass `-backend-config=FILE` or `KEY=VALUE` to init.
After changing the backend, run `terraform init -migrate-state` to copy state across.
Supply credentials by env vars; `-backend-config` values land in `.terraform/` and plan files.
A `cloud` block replaces `backend` for HCP Terraform; never use both.
notes.tip: Variables in a backend block are a common wrong answer. Remote state is kept in memory, not written to local disk, except when saving to the backend fails.

notes.title: Detect and fix drift
notes.gist: Drift means real infrastructure no longer matches state; inspect it with a refresh-only plan, then accept it or overwrite it.
points: `terraform plan -refresh-only` shows what changed outside Terraform and changes nothing.
`terraform apply -refresh-only` writes reality into state without touching resources.
A normal `terraform apply` reverts the drift to match config.
Prefer it over legacy `terraform refresh`, which overwrites state with no review.
`-replace=ADDR` rebuilds a degraded resource; `-refresh=false` skips refresh and can miss drift.
notes.tip: Decide the direction. Keep the manual change: update config, then `apply -refresh-only`. Reject it: plain `apply`. HCP Terraform drift detection needs Standard or Premium.

`removed` (1.7+) with `lifecycle { destroy = false }` drops it from state, keeps it running.

One `backend` block, no variables in it; use `-backend-config` for partial config.
Change backends with `terraform init -migrate-state`.
`plan -refresh-only` shows drift; `apply -refresh-only` accepts it into state.
`moved` renames without recreate; `removed` with `destroy = false` forgets without deleting.
traps: Using variables inside a `backend` block, or both `backend` and `cloud` blocks.
Renaming a resource label without a `moved` block, which plans destroy and create.
Treating CLI workspaces as a security boundary or the same as HCP workspaces.

cards.q: Which backend is the default, and where does it write state?
cards.a: The `local` backend. It writes `terraform.tfstate` in the working directory.

cards.q: When does Terraform lock state, and do you have to ask for it?
cards.a: Automatically, on every operation that could write state, if the backend supports locking. No message is shown.

cards.q: Which command clears a stuck state lock, and whose lock should you use it on?
cards.a: `terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID`. Use it only for your own lock.

cards.q: How many `backend` blocks can a configuration have, and how do you supply values left out of it?
cards.a: One. Leave values out and pass `-backend-config=FILE` or `KEY=VALUE` to `terraform init` (partial configuration).

cards.q: Which command copies existing state to a new backend after you change the `backend` block?
cards.a: `terraform init -migrate-state`.

cards.q: Which command shows drift without changing anything, and which one writes reality into state?
cards.a: `terraform plan -refresh-only` shows drift; `terraform apply -refresh-only` writes reality into state without touching resources.

cards.q: Which block renames a resource without recreating it, and which one drops it from state but keeps it running?
cards.a: `moved` (1.1+) renames without recreating; `removed` (1.7+) with `lifecycle { destroy = false }` forgets it without deleting.

cards.q: Trap: can a `backend` block use variables, or can a configuration hold both `backend` and `cloud` blocks?
cards.a: No to both. A `cloud` block replaces `backend` for HCP Terraform, and a backend block cannot use variables.

cards.q: Trap: what does the plan show if you rename a resource label without a `moved` block?
cards.a: A destroy and a create. With a `moved` block the plan shows a move and no change.

cards.q: Trap: are CLI workspaces a security boundary, or the same as HCP Terraform workspaces?
cards.a: No to both. CLI workspaces only split state under one backend; they are unsuitable when environments need separate credentials or access control.

cards.q: Which S3 backend setting enables state locking, and what is deprecated?
cards.a: `use_lockfile = true`. S3 locking through DynamoDB is deprecated in favour of the S3 lock file.

cards.q: What is the default `-lock-timeout`, and what does `-lock-timeout=60s` do?
cards.a: The default `0s` fails immediately when state is locked; `-lock-timeout=60s` waits for the lock.

cards.q: Drift found: how do you keep the manual change, and how do you reject it?
cards.a: Keep: update config, then `apply -refresh-only`. Reject: plain `terraform apply` reverts the drift to match config.

cards.q: Which workspace can never be deleted, and which expression returns the current workspace name?
cards.a: The `default` workspace cannot be deleted; `terraform.workspace` returns the current name.
